      ./codex-session-01a0a6bd-2550-76a1-b623-75259209bfe3.md:31360:      /home/mm29942/.harw/profiles/default/sessions/655d3b23-9894-4094-abe0-5c141207ea51.jsonl:116:{"session_id":"655d3b23-9894-4094-abe0-5c141207ea51","thread":"cli-session:655d3b23-9894-4094-abe0-5c141207ea51","sequence":115,"recorded_at":"2026-09-15T07:49:01.184958525Z","kind":"item","payload":{"type":"tool_result","id":"e1e45c27-ff01-402b-b669-574001b69e47","call_id":"call_mVeJGZj58KdrCGx5tI5wR5JQ","result":{"status":"success","value":" 7.1 What sgh-s3ice is\n\n`sgh-s3ice` is a **separate runtime product** inside the workspace, like\nvectory and not like a library that one participant happens to link.\n\nIt runs as its own daemon (`sgh-s3iced`, default port `18182`), it has its own\nconfig, error, registry and storage crates (12 crates in `sgh-s3ice/crates/`),\nand it exposes its capability over MCP under the `s3ice.*` namespace\n(`sgh-s3ice-mcp`, built on the `sgh-mcp-build` product-server facade).\n\nIts subject is analytical storage:\n\n- the Iceberg REST catalog connection (`sgh-s3ice-catalog::OrgCatalog`)\n- org-scoped namespaces and tables\n- Arrow/Parquet schema conversion and writing\n- object-store access\n- query/read paths over stored tables\n- the `s3ice.*` MCP tool surface\n\n## 7.2 What sgh-s3ice owns\n\n`sgh-s3ice` owns, for **every** participant:\n\n- catalog identity: which namespace and which table a tenant's data lives in\n- catalog credentials and their refresh (OAuth token refresh lives in\n  `sgh-s3ice-catalog::TokenRefresher`, once, not per consumer)\n- table lifecycle: create, describe, list, delete\n- append/read semantics and Parquet writer configuration\n- org resolution before any storage access — `sgh-s3ice-registry`'s\n  `OrgContext` typestate gate resolves the calling principal's org *before* a\n  handler may touch backend state\n\n## 7.3 How sgh-flow consumes it — the reference pattern\n\n`sgh-flow` does not open an Iceberg catalog. It calls the product.\n\n`crates/sgh-flow-s3ice::McpS3iceAdapter` is the whole surface, and it is thin\non purpose: every method is one JSON-RPC `tools/call` against the daemon.\nEight tools, no local catalog state (`crates/sgh-flow-s3ice/src/adapter.rs`):\n\n- `s3ice.register_namespace`\n- `s3ice.create_table`\n- `s3ice.describe_table`\n- `s3ice.list_tables`\n- `s3ice.get`\n- `s3ice.append`\n- `s3ice.delete_table`\n- `s3ice.drop_namespace`\n\nThat is the shape a participant's storage dependency is supposed to have: a\ntyped adapter over a named tool set, no `iceberg::Catalog` import, no\nwarehouse URI, no Parquet writer properties on the consumer side.\n\n## 7.4 What sgh-s3ice must not absorb\n\nIt should not own:\n\n- workflow or approval truth\n- business meaning of the rows it stores\n- tenant authority (it enforces org scoping; it does not decide org policy)\n- retrieval/embedding semantics — that is vectory\n- key custody — that is secureHUB\n\nIt is storage substrate with an org gate, not a second platform.\n\n## 7.5 Anti-drift: a participant-local Iceberg rebuild is an architecture error\n\nThis deserves its own statement because it is not a style preference.\n\nA participant that builds its own `CatalogBuilder` / `RestCatalog` wiring, its\nown token refresh and its own Parquet writer has forked the catalog layer. The\nconsequences are not hypothetical: catalog credentials then live in two places,\nnamespace conventions drift apart, org scoping is enforced twice with two\ndifferent definitions of \"scoped\", and a schema fix has to be made twice by\nsomeone who has to know both copies exist.\n\n**This state exists today** in `sgh-acct/crates/sgh-acct-iceberg`:\n`handler.rs` imports `iceberg::{Catalog, CatalogBuilder}`,\n`RestCatalog`/`RestCatalogBuilder` with `REST_CATALOG_PROP_URI` /\n`REST_CATALOG_PROP_WAREHOUSE`, and drives `ParquetWriterBuilder` with its own\n`WriterProperties` — i.e. it reimplements what `sgh-s3iced` already serves.\n\nIt is recorded here as a **condition to be repaired**, not as a permitted\nvariant. The target is that `sgh-acct` reaches Iceberg exactly the way\n`sgh-flow` does: through an MCP adapter over `s3ice.*`.\n\n---\n\n## 8. sgh-acct — the invoice-accounting participant, not a second platform\n\n## 8.1 What sgh-acct is\n\n`sgh-acct` is a **participant**: a domain product that runs beside the\nplatform under the platform's participant contract.\n\n- process: `sgh-acctd`\n- manifest: `sgh-acct/participant.toml` (port `4610`, subject kind `invoice`,\n  route prefix `/acct`, own vault)\n- own database: `acctdb`\n- MCP namespace: `acct`\n- 6 crates in `sgh-acct/crates/` (config, db, error, iceberg, service, daemon)\n\nThe manifest is the single source for its systemd unit, env block and\ninfrastructure needs, and it deliberately contains **no** UUIDs — identities\nare derived or read back, never transcribed (the parser actively rejects\nUUID-shaped values). That rule is the same one chapter 14 states platform-wide.\n\n## 8.2 What sgh-acct owns\n\n`sgh-acct` owns the **operational invoice-data truth**:\n\n- invoice items, positions and their accounting assignment (Kontierung)\n- the master data the assignment resolves against: `sachkonto`, `kreditor`,\n  `cost_center`, `segment`, `department` — all in `acctdb`\n- the accounting-domain logic that turns a normalized invoice into booked lines\n- the `acct.*` MCP tools that expose those capabilities\n- its own agent wiring for AI-assisted accounting proposals\n\nThis is the strong, legitimate core of the participant: nobody else should\nhold the Kontierung tables or the accounting rules that read them.\n\n## 8.3 What sgh-acct must not become\n\nIt must not become:\n\n- **its own decision/audit truth.** Approval, decision history and audit\n  remain platform-owned. sgh-acct may *read* decisions; it does not become the\n  place where \"what was approved\" is authoritatively kept, because a second\n  authority for that question means neither answer can be trusted.\n- **its own Iceberg catalog.** See 7.5 — `sgh-acct-iceberg` is the concrete\n  drift to unwind, not the pattern to extend.\n- **its own vector-store operator.** Store lifecycle, embedding and retrieval\n  stay in vectory; sgh-acct is a consumer of retrieval, not a runner of it.\n- **the place where platform-wide tenant decisions are made.** Which org a\n  request belongs to, and whether that claim is trustworthy, is a platform\n  question. A participant enforces the scope it is handed; it does not invent\n  it.\n\n## 8.4 Tenant scope is verified, not asserted\n\n`sgh-acctd` derives the tenant scope from the signed `X-SGH-*` edge context, not\nfrom the request body. `verified_edge_scope_from_headers`\n(`sgh-acct/crates/sgh-acctd/src/app.rs`) checks an HMAC-SHA256 proof over the\norganisation, subject and timestamp, enforces a timestamp window, and is wired\ninto the `/mcp` handler before any tool dispatch. An empty or missing secret\nfails **closed** (`EdgeContextError::SecretNotConfigured`) — there is no bypass.\n\n`params._meta.organization_id` still travels in the JSON-RPC body, but only as a\n**consistency check** against the verified scope. It is no longer the source of\nthe tenant identity.\n\nThis closes what was previously recorded here as an open gap, and it makes the\nparticipant obey the same rule chapter 4.2 sets for a product boundary:\ncredentials terminate at the edge, signed context crosses.\n\nTwo things this does **not** cover, and they belong to operations rather than\ncode: whether `sgh-acctd` is reachable without traversing the edge at all is a\nnetwork-topology question, and the guarantee is only as strong as the secret\nprovisioning behind it. A fail-closed check protects against forged headers; it\ncannot protect against a secret that was never rotated or was copied somewhere\nit does not belong.\n\n## 8.5 Why sgh-acct is complex even as \"just a participant\"\n\nIts difficulty is not the accounting arithmetic. It is that it sits at the\nintersection of every cross-cutting invariant at once: multi-tenancy and RLS\nover `acctdb`, AI proposals that must stay proposals, a domain model fed by\n`xmlinvoice` normalization, analytical storage it must obtain from `sgh-s3ice`\nrather than build, and secrets it must obtain from secureHUB rather than hold.\n\nEvery one of those is a place where the cheap local implementation looks\nsmaller than the correct delegated one.\n\n---\n\n## 9. Multi-tenancy — not a feature, a system-wide invariant\n\n## 9.1 What multi-tenancy means here\n\nMulti-tenancy means multiple organizations share the same platform while data,\npermissions, workflow visibility, and side effects remain strictly isolated\nunless an explicitly authorized cross-org mechanism exists.\n\nThis affects nearly everything:\n\n- principals and claims\n- DB transactions\n- event streams\n- vector stores\n- secret storage\n- audit visibility\n- worker permissions\n- admin surfaces\n\n## 9.2 Why this is hard\n\nA system is not safely multi-tenant just because tables have an\n`organization_id` column.\n\nTrue multi-tenancy requires that:\n\n- the effective org context is derived from trusted identity,\n- every read/write path respects that context,\n- runtime participants do not accept forged org scope,\n- stores and caches do not bleed across org boundaries,\n- retrieval systems and AI helpers do not accidentally surface cross-tenant data.\n\nThis is especially important when multiple products (`sgh-flow`, `vectory`,\n`secureHUB`) participate in one end-to-end workflow.\n\n---\n\n## 10. RLS — database enforcement of tenant isolation\n\n## 10.1 What RLS is in this platform\n\nRLS (Row-Level Security) is the database-side mechanism that enforces which\nrows are visible or writable for the effective organization/principal context.\n\nIt is the difference between:\n\n- \"the application tried to filter correctly\"\n- and\n- \"the database itself rejects out-of-scope row access\"\n\n## 10.2 Why RLS matters so much here\n\nThis platform has enough moving parts that application-only filtering is too\nfragile. Once there are:\n\n- background workers,\n- admin tools,\n- direct import paths,\n- AI-driven commands,\n- participant services,\n- retrieval systems,\n- and multiple databases,\n\nthen tenancy protection must have a DB-enforced layer.\n\n## 10.3 The intended RLS discipline\n\nThe important architectural discipline is:\n\n- derive org scope from verified principal context,\n- enter a scoped DB transaction/session,\n- let DB policies enforce row visibility,\n- avoid pretending a plain SQL `WHERE organization_id = ...` is sufficient.\n\nThat makes RLS part of the trust boundary, not just an optimization.\n\n---\n\n## 11. Typestate — compile-time lifecycle enforcement for state-rich flows\n\n## 11.1 What typestate means here\n\nTypestate means representing lifecycle stages in Rust types so invalid\ntransitions do not compile.\n\nExamples of the general idea:\n\n- `RawReceived`\n- `RawPersisted`\n- `XmlValidated`\n- `JsonMaterialized`\n- `DerivedPersisted`\n- `Snapshotted`\n\nThe purpose is to encode process guarantees in the type system instead of only\nin comments or runtime conditionals.\n\n## 11.2 Where typestate fits best in this platform\n\nTypestate is especially appropriate for:\n\n- ingest pipelines\n- approval pipelines\n- validated-versus-unvalidated transitions\n- operations that must not happen before persistence/verification\n- security-sensitive state progression\n\n## 11.3 Where typestate belongs conceptually\n\n- In `xmlinvoice`, typestate may be useful for **document transformation\n  correctness** if the library has clearly staged parse/validate/write flows.\n- In `sgh-flow`, typestate is even more important for **workflow lifecycle\n  correctness**, because that is where persistence, snapshots, approvals,\n  and side effects are coordinated.\n\nThe main architectural point is that typestate for the **business process**\nbelongs closer to `sgh-flow` than to `xmlinvoice`.\n\n## 11.4 Why typestate is important here\n\nThis platform has enough high-value transitions that runtime booleans like\n`is_validated` or `status = \"ready\"` can become too weak and too easy to misuse.\nTypestate makes illegal states harder to represent and illegal transitions\nharder to implement by accident.\n\n---\n\n## 12. AI is not one feature here — it is a cross-cutting complexity multiplier\n\nAI in this platform is not only \"call a model and get text back\".\nIt interacts with:\n\n- invoice extraction/proposals\n- worker flows and MCP tools\n- vectory retrieval\n- secret handling / model credentials\n- audit and approval processes\n- tenant isolation\n- durable write discipline\n\nThat means AI multiplies the importance of all existing boundaries:\n\n- Rust must remain the authority for writes and validation.\n- Tenant scoping must survive every AI-assisted action.\n- Retrieval must not leak across orgs.\n- Secrets and model credentials must have a real custody story.\n- Proposed actions must not silently become authoritative truth.\n\nSo the platform complexity is not just \"AI + app\". It is **AI inside a\nmulti-tenant, RLS-backed, retrieval-aware, security-sensitive financial-ish\nsystem**.\n\n---\n\n## 13. Boundary summary\n\n## sgh-flow owns\n- workflow truth\n- orchestration\n- principal/org execution context\n- persistence and side effects\n- approvals and eventing\n- integration governance\n\n## vectory owns\n- embeddings/retrieval/index/search behavior\n- vector-store lifecycle\n- retrieval MCP surface\n- store-specific operational semantics\n\n## secureHUB owns\n- tenant-scoped keys and secrets\n- envelope encryption/decryption\n- crypto policy and custody\n- trust-boundary auth/signature patterns\n- crypto audit surfaces\n\n## xmlinvoice owns\n- invoice parsing/normalization/validation/writing\n- canonical invoice-domain structures\n- format/profile correctness\n\n## sgh-s3ice owns\n- Iceberg REST catalog access and catalog credentials/token refresh\n- org-scoped namespaces and table lifecycle\n- Arrow/Parquet schema conversion, writing and object-store access\n- the `s3ice.*` MCP tool surface for every participant\n\n## sgh-acct owns\n- operational invoice-data truth in `acctdb` (items/positions, Kontierung)\n- accounting master data: sachkonto, kreditor, cost center, segment, department\n- accounting-domain logic and the `acct.*` MCP tool surface\n- its participant manifest as the single source for unit/env/infrastructure\n\n## cross-cutting invariants\n- multi-tenancy\n- RLS discipline\n- typed/state-safe transitions\n- Rust-owned durable truth\n- explicit runtime contracts between products\n- derived-not-transcribed identity across product boundaries\n- credentials terminate at the edge; only signed context crosses\n\n---\n\n## 14. Non-goals and anti-drift rules\n\n### Do not let xmlinvoice become a mini-platform\nNo DB, no tenant lookup, no vector search, no orchestration ownership.\n\n### Do not let vectory become workflow truth\nNo silent ownership of approvals, tenant authority, or business lifecycle.\n\n### Do not let secureHUB become a vague crypto dumping ground\nIt should own concrete KMS/vault/trust responsibilities, not random unrelated\nsecurity-adjacent code.\n\n### Do not let a participant rebuild the Iceberg catalog\nAnalytical storage is reached through `sgh-s3iced`'s `s3ice.*` tools, the way\n`crates/sgh-flow-s3ice::McpS3iceAdapter` reaches it. A participant-local\n`RestCatalog` plus Parquet writer is not a faster variant of that, it is a fork\nof the catalog layer — duplicated credentials, drifting namespace conventions,\nand two places that must both be fixed by someone who knows both exist.\n`sgh-acct/crates/sgh-acct-iceberg` is currently in exactly that state and is to\nbe unwound, not imitated.\n\n### Do not let sgh-acct grow into a second platform\nIt owns invoice-accounting data and rules. Decision/audit truth, vector-store\noperation, catalog operation and platform-wide tenant authority stay outside\nit. A participant enforces the scope it is handed; it does not become the place\nthat defines it.\n\n### Do not accept an unverified tenant claim as tenant scope\nAn `organization_id` lifted straight out of a request body is an assertion by\nthe caller, not a proof. `sgh-acctd` used to do exactly that; it now derives the\nscope from the HMAC-verified `X-SGH-*` edge context and keeps the body value only\nas a consistency check (chapter 8.4). The rule stands for every future\nparticipant: verified scope from the start, because \"the caller told us\" fails\nsilently and in the tenant's favour.\n\n### Do not let AI become the authority\nAI may assist, rank, propose, summarize, or route; typed Rust boundaries and\nscoped persistence remain authoritative.\n\n### Do not read ownership from a crate name\nA `sgh-flow-` prefix records where a crate was first written, not who owns it.\n`crates/sgh-flow-s3ice` is a fully generic s3ice adapter — no `sgh_flow::`\nreference anywhere in its source, and its only dependencies are the shared\n`sgh-mcp-client`, `sgh-identity-core`, `sgh-s3ice-protocol` and\n`sgh-provenance`. Any participant can depend on it directly.\n\nThat misreading has already cost this workspace a five-thousand-line parallel\nimplementation of an Iceberg catalog. Ownership is settled by reading the\ndependency list, never by reading the name. When a name genuinely misleads,\nrenaming the crate is cheaper than the duplicate it will otherwise cause.\n\n### Do not rebuild what already exists unwired\nThe dominant failure mode in this workspace is not missing code — it is code\nthat exists and was never connected. `InvoiceActionsService` (740 lines) and\n`invoice_list.rs` (742 lines) were complete and instantiated nowhere;\n`PlatformClient::fetch_infra_token` was finished and had no caller;\n`IcebergRuntimeCredentials` carried `#[allow(dead_code)]` while the thing meant\nto fill it was being planned from scratch.\n\nBefore writing anything new, the order is: does it already exist here, possibly\nunwired — is there a shared crate that does it — does it exist in the platform\nand can it move — and only then, write it. An agent told to build X will build\nX; it will not spontaneously check whether X is already sitting there.\n\n### Exactly one writer per table, at every moment\nWhen a table exists in two databases during a migration, exactly one side may\nwrite it at any given time, and the switch of that right is a discrete,\nreversible step — never a gradual state where both write and a sync reconciles\nafterwards.\n\nThe subtle failure is the inverse of the obvious one. A replication exclusion\nthat protects a participant's own writes silently becomes a data-loss path the\nmoment that participant has not actually written anything: the rows never\narrive, the row-count check skips the table by design, and nothing reports a\nproblem. An exclusion list is a claim about who writes — verify the claim\nagainst the data before trusting it.\n\n### Do not let identity values become hand-maintained\nIdentifiers that another system owns are derived from their defining inputs or\nread back from that system's own response — never transcribed, and never\n\"corrected\" by hand to make something start. A value a human can adjust under\ntime pressure will eventually be adjusted, and a plausible-looking wrong value\nis indistinguishable from a right one until something far downstream refuses\nit.\n\n### Do not treat a compiling test suite as a passing one\n`clippy --tests` compiles tests; it does not run them. A suite that is only\never compiled gives full type safety and no behavioural safety, and lets\nassertions drift away from the code they describe — including away from the\ndoc comment directly above it. Tests must actually execute, and the suite must\nbe deterministic enough that a failure means something: parallel tests that\nmutate process environment produce a failure set that changes between runs, and\nwhile that is true no result can be trusted.\n\n### A variable is not provisioned because it is written down somewhere\nThe question is never \"is the variable set\" but \"is the file it is set in loaded\nby the process that reads it\". Two env files legitimately coexist here and must\nnot be confused:\n\n- **Runtime env** — `<prefix>/etc/sgh-flow/sgh-flow.env`. The only file the\n  installed units load: `cli::acct::install_acct` renders `sgh-acctd.service`\n  with exactly that path as its `EnvironmentFile`\n  (`apps/sgh-flow/src/cli/acct.rs:151-160`), and `sgh-flowd` resolves the same\n  file (`apps/sgh-flow/src/runtime.rs:304`). A variable a daemon needs at\n  startup must be here or the daemon does not start.\n- **Tool env** — e.g. `<prefix>/etc/sgh-acct/sgh-acctd.env`. Read by `make`\n  targets and operator tooling. No unit loads it.\n\n`SGH_ACCT_AUTH_TOKEN` and `SGH_ACCT_DATABASE_URL` were written to the tool env\nonly; `sgh_acct_config::AppConfig::from_env` would have refused the start. Both\n`cli/ensure_acct_auth_secret.rs` and `cli/ensure_acct_database_url.rs` now write\none planned value to *both* targets and verify the write afterwards\n(`ensure_acct_database_url.rs:135-136`, `:252-290`). The same trap sits in\n`.env.example`: nothing copies it anywhere, so an entry there is documentation,\nnever delivery. This confusion survived five review passes — check the loader,\nnot the line.\n\n### Responsibility follows the process tree, not the name\nWhich process reads a variable is decided by who spawns whom, not by the prefix\nthe variable carries. `SMART_ACC_ACCT_DSN` reads as \"ACCT\" and was therefore put\ninto `sgh-acct/deploy/sgh-acctd.service` as an `Environment=` line — but its only\nreader is `sgh-acct/python_agent/smart_accounter.py:2106`, whose ancestry is\n`sgh-flowd` → `sgh-flow-agentd` (`SMART_*` allowlist,\n`apps/sgh-flow/src/services/python_agent.rs:477-500`) → `python -m\nsmart_accounter` (`apps/sgh-flow/src/bin/sgh-flow-agentd.rs:675-686`).\n`sgh-acctd` does not appear in that chain, so the line did nothing; the unit now\ncarries an explicit \"NICHT HIER SETZEN\" note instead\n(`sgh-acct/deploy/sgh-acctd.service:24`). This is the sibling of *Do not read\nownership from a crate name*: trace the spawn chain, then decide.\n\n### Do not cite a paragraph you have not looked up\nFour invented references have already been found in this tree. Three cited\n\"CONTRACT.md §7\" for the codex-credential decision at a time when the word\n\"codex\" did not appear in `CONTRACT.md` at all (recorded in\n`sgh-acct/NACHWEIS-3.md:268`; §7 only gained the matching Amendment\n2026-08-12, `sgh-acct/CONTRACT.md:222-229`). One cited \"Contract-Master §5\" in\n`sgh-acct/deploy/sgh-acctd.service` for rendering rather than installing the\nunit — §5 is the MCP wire contract (`sgh-acct/CONTRACT.md:153`); the file now\nsays so itself (`:5-7`).\n\nThe damage is not cosmetic. An unverifiable justification invites the next\neditor to decide again, and that overwrote a predecessor's correct decision:\n`codex-credential` was moved onto `/acct`, where `sgh-acctd` answers `501 Not\nImplemented` (`sgh-acct/crates/sgh-acctd/src/app/worker_api.rs:308`) and the\nworker raises on anything but `404`. An unsupported citation is worse than none.\nIf no paragraph backs the claim, write *that* down instead.\n\n### Do not create anything that gets no caller the same day\nInfrastructure here runs ahead of its wiring — tables before writers, endpoints\nbefore feeders, a listener before its configuration\n(`sgh-acct/NACHWEIS-3.md:488`). Finished, documented and tested, yet unwired:\n`reclaim_zombies` (`sgh-acct/crates/sgh-acct-db/src/job_store.rs:592`),\n`insert_extracted_lines`\n(`sgh-acct/crates/sgh-acct-db/src/repositories/invoice_items.rs:248`), the\nthe `_acct_meta` write mechanics\n(`scripts/acctdb-sync.sh:851` `write_acceptance_meta`, `:897`\n`write_skipped_orphans_meta`; the table stood empty until the path was first run\nby hand), `AgentSpec` in the participant manifest — \"a pure\ndeclaration … no runtime wiring reads it yet\" by its own doc comment\n(`crates/sgh-participant/src/onboarding.rs:75-82`) — and a `--verify` mode that\nwas built and never run (`sgh-acct/NACHWEIS-5.md:126-138`).\n\nThe necessary qualification: \"has no caller\" is a *question*, not a verdict. A\nrepository method without a caller may be legitimate surface. The test that\ndecides is the one stated in `sgh-acct/NACHWEIS-6.md:670` — not \"does this\nfunction have a caller\", but **\"is there a reader that comes up empty without\nthis writer\"**. If yes, the missing wiring is a defect today; if no, the code is\npremature and should not have been written yet.\n\n---\n\n## 15. The real complexity statement\n\nThis platform is complex because it combines, in one architecture:\n\n- a multi-tenant workflow engine\n- database-enforced row isolation\n- a separate retrieval/vector-memory product\n- AI-assisted processing and tool use\n- a planned PQC-capable KMS/vault/trust system\n- pure but non-trivial invoi\n\n[fs.read: Ausgabe gekürzt auf 24000 Bytes (Bytes 16600..40600 von 41003); weiterlesen mit offset=40600]"},"duration_ms":3,"trust":"untrusted"}}

Because there is only one\nverification secret, the shared value must *be* sgh-flow's session-signing\nsecret — provisioning may distribute it, but must never rotate it as a side\neffect.\n\nTwo properties of this arrangement are easy to get wrong and expensive to\ndiagnose: an **empty** secret on the participant side disables validation\nentirely rather than failing closed, and a mismatched secret rejects every\nendpoint uniformly, which reads like an outage rather than a configuration\nerror.\n\n## 4.3 What vectory owns\n\n`vectory` should own:\n\n- vector-store definitions and lifecycle\n- embedding/index/search mechanics\n- retrieval ranking and lookup semantics\n- store-level operational behavior\n- retrieval-specific persistence inside its own product domain\n- MCP tools that expose retrieval/search capabilities\n\nA very important aspect of complexity here is that vectory is not \"just AI\".\nIt is infrastructure for **machine-usable memory and search**.\n\nThat includes the platform problem of maintaining **multiple stores with\nseparate meanings**, for example decision memory versus other knowledge stores.\nThe moment the platform has its own decision/history memory, vectory becomes\npart of the system's long-lived reasoning substrate, not just a search helper.\n\n## 4.4 What vectory should not become\n\n`vectory` should not become the place that owns:\n\n- overall workflow truth\n- approval truth\n- authoritative tenant/process state\n- arbitrary business side effects\n- free-form policy enforcement that belongs at the edge/application layer\n\nIt may perform retrieval and perhaps structured lookup, but it should not turn\ninto a second workflow platform.\n\n## 4.5 Why vectory is technically complex\n\n### Separate product complexity\nIt is independently deployed and operated.\n\n### Separate data complexity\nIt may maintain its own DB and store topology, with org-scoped resources and\nstore provisioning concerns.\n\n### Search semantics complexity\nVector search is not ordinary filtering. It brings ranking, embeddings,\napproximate similarity, store-specific schemas, and operational drift between\nindex content and source-of-truth business data.\n\n### Runtime contract complexity\nIts MCP/HTTP surface is fragile in the good sense: tool names and argument\nshapes are contracts.\n\n### Tenant safety complexity\nA retrieval system can leak across org boundaries if scoping, auth, or store\nregistration is even slightly wrong.\n\nIn other words: vectory is its own subsystem because platform retrieval with\norg isolation and stable MCP contracts is inherently a serious systems problem.\n\n---\n\n## 5. secureHUB — org-scoped KMS, vault, trust boundary, and PQC policy center\n\n## 5.1 What secureHUB is\n\n`secureHUB` is the intended **security product** of the platform. Not just a\nutility library and not just a secret box.\n\nIts target role is to own:\n\n- tenant-scoped key management\n- envelope encryption and decryption services\n- secret storage and retrieval\n- key versioning and custody\n- cryptographic policy per tenant / keyset\n- trust-token or signature support\n- audit around cryptographic operations\n- a fail-closed principal/auth pattern for participant services\n\n## 5.2 What makes secureHUB different from ordinary config-secret handling\n\nThis is not merely about storing an API key more safely.\nThe intended problem space includes:\n\n- KMS-like responsibilities\n- secrets-vault responsibilities\n- organization-scoped isolation\n- cryptographic policy management\n- participant trust and verification\n- high-assurance handling of financial-data-adjacent cryptography\n\nThat is a much broader scope than \"encrypt a field before writing it\".\n\n## 5.3 PQC is not decorative here\n\nThe secureHUB scope explicitly includes **post-quantum cryptography policy**.\nThat matters because the system is designed around configurable choices such as:\n\n- ML-KEM levels\n- ML-DSA levels\n- SLH-DSA choices\n- AEAD choices like XChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-256-GCM-SIV\n- tenant-specific policy rather than a single hardcoded global preset\n\nThis raises the complexity materially because the system must handle:\n\n- algorithm selection\n- policy persistence\n- compatibility rules\n- envelope validation\n- key lifecycle and rewrap concerns\n- auditability of crypto choices\n- safe defaults without pretending there is one universal correct profile\n\n## 5.4 secureHUB is also a trust-boundary project\n\nsecureHUB is not only about cryptography; it is also about **auth correctness**.\nThe architecture direction is that participant services should use a\nfail-closed, verified principal model rather than trusting forged or weakly\nvalidated metadata.\n\nThat means secureHUB touches:\n\n- principal extraction behavior\n- service-to-service trust\n- signature verification\n- auth token semantics\n- how org scope is derived and enforced\n\nSo its scope cuts across both security and runtime architecture.\n\n### Exactly one system identity per deployment\n\nsecureHUB recognises a **single** durable system principal per instance. Every\ntyped system-secret operation — put, resolve, lookup, reconcile — compares the\ncaller's JWT subject for *exact equality* against that one configured identity.\nThere is no list, no per-participant identity, and no fallback: a mismatch is a\nbare `403` that names nothing, which makes this one of the least\nself-explanatory failure modes in the platform.\n\nThat identity is not a random value to be copied around. It is **derived\ndeterministically** from the deployment tuple `service_name`, `instance_id`,\nand `environment`, and the row it identifies is unique on exactly that tuple.\nAnything that needs the identity should therefore *compute* it from the tuple\nrather than store a copy, because a computed value cannot go stale while a\nstored one silently can.\n\nThe derivation necessarily exists twice: `secureHUB` is a separate cargo\nworkspace, so no crate can be shared with `apps/sgh-flow`. The contract between\nthe two copies is a **pinned test vector held identically on both sides** — if\neither changes the namespace, the separator, or the field order, its own test\nfails without needing the other side to compile.\n\n### The vault is authoritative, not the disk\n\nBoot-time reconciliation looks a secret up before provisioning it. Plaintext\ncredential material on disk is therefore required only on a genuinely first\nboot, or after the secureHUB record has been wiped — not on every start. This\nis what makes it legitimate to remove plaintext credentials from a host once\nthey are sealed, which is the entire point of having a vault.\n\n## 5.5 What secureHUB should not absorb\n\nsecureHUB should not become:\n\n- the business workflow engine\n- the invoice parser/normalizer\n- the vector retrieval engine\n- the UI/backend orchestration center\n\nIt should own the security boundary, not every feature that uses security.\n\n## 5.6 Why secureHUB is technically complex\n\nBecause it combines all of these in one boundary:\n\n1. tenant-scoped storage\n2. key management\n3. cryptographic policy\n4. trusted service auth patterns\n5. auditability\n6. future migration pressure from current local-key patterns\n\nA system that does KMS + vault + participant trust + PQC policy is not a minor\nsubsystem. It is effectively security infrastructure.\n\n---\n\n## 6. xmlinvoice — pure invoice-domain engine, not a workflow platform\n\n## 6.1 What xmlinvoice is\n\n`xmlinvoice` should remain a **pure invoice-domain library**.\n\nIts role is to own:\n\n- document type/profile detection\n- parsing invoice XML\n- normalization into canonical invoice structures\n- semantic validation\n- invoice creation/writer support\n- canonical JSON representation of normalized invoice data\n\n## 6.2 What xmlinvoice should own very clearly\n\n`xmlinvoice` is the right place for:\n\n- syntax and profile logic\n- invoice model fidelity\n- schema/profile transformation\n- invoice-specific validation rules\n- stable normalized output contracts\n\nThe key architectural idea is that `NormalizedInvoice` or an equivalent\ncanonical model is a stable **document-domain contract**, not a workflow state.\n\n## 6.3 What xmlinvoice must not absorb\n\nIt should not own:\n\n- DB persistence\n- RLS/tenant context\n- vector store lookup\n- AI orchestration\n- approval lifecycle\n- snapshot governance\n- object storage policy\n- cross-service process sequencing\n\nThose belong to the surrounding platform, mainly `sgh-flow`.\n\n## 6.4 Why xmlinvoice is still complex even though it should stay \"pure\"\n\nPurity does not mean simplicity.\n\nIt still must correctly handle:\n\n- multiple e-invoice formats/profiles\n- parse/normalize/write correctness\n- validation semantics\n- canonical JSON stability\n- lossy versus lossless transformation questions\n- creation DTOs versus stable normalized models\n\nSo xmlinvoice is a focused library, but it is a serious one.\nIts complexity is domain correctness, not systems orchestration.\n\n---\n\n## 7. sgh-s3ice — Iceberg catalog and Parquet storage as a shared runtime product\n\n## 7.1 What sgh-s3ice is\n\n`sgh-s3ice` is a **separate runtime product** inside the workspace, like\nvectory and not like a library that one participant happens to link.\n\nIt runs as its own daemon (`sgh-s3iced`, default port `18182`), it has its own\nconfig, error, registry and storage crates (12 crates in `sgh-s3ice/crates/`),\nand it exposes its capability over MCP under the `s3ice.*` namespace\n(`sgh-s3ice-mcp`, built on the `sgh-mcp-build` product-server facade).\n\nIts subject is analytical storage:\n\n- the Iceberg REST catalog connection (`sgh-s3ice-catalog::OrgCatalog`)\n- org-scoped namespaces and tables\n- Arrow/Parquet schema conversion and writing\n- object-store access\n- query/read paths over stored tables\n- the `s3ice.*` MCP tool surface\n\n## 7.2 What sgh-s3ice owns\n\n`sgh-s3ice` owns, for **every** participant:\n\n- catalog identity: which namespace and which table a tenant's data lives in\n- catalog credentials and their refresh (OAuth token refresh lives in\n  `sgh-s3ice-catalog::TokenRefresher`, once, not per consumer)\n- table lifecycle: create, describe, list, delete\n- append/read semantics and Parquet writer configuration\n- org resolution before any storage access — `sgh-s3ice-registry`'s\n  `OrgContext` typestate gate resolves the calling principal's org *before* a\n  handler may touch backend state\n\n## 7.3 How sgh-flow consumes it — the reference pattern\n\n`sgh-flow` does not open an Iceberg catalog. It calls the product.\n\n`crates/sgh-flow-s3ice::McpS3iceAdapter` is the whole surface, and it is thin\non purpose: every method is one JSON-RPC `tools/call` against the daemon.\nEight tools, no local catalog state (`crates/sgh-flow-s3ice/src/adapter.rs`):\n\n- `s3ice.register_namespace`\n- `s3ice.create_table`\n- `s3ice.describe_table`\n- `s3ice.list_tables`\n- `s3ice.get`\n- `s3ice.append`\n- `s3ice.delete_table`\n- `s3ice.drop_namespace`\n\nThat is the shape a participant's storage dependency is supposed to have: a\ntyped adapter over a named tool set, no `iceberg::Catalog` import, no\nwarehouse URI, no Parquet writer properties on the consumer side.\n\n## 7.4 What sgh-s3ice must not absorb\n\nIt should not own:\n\n- workflow or approval truth\n- business meaning of the rows it stores\n- tenant authority (it enforces org scoping; it does not decide org policy)\n- retrieval/embedding semantics — that is vectory\n- key custody — that is secureHUB\n\nIt is storage substrate with an org gate, not a second platform.\n\n## 7.5 Anti-drift: a participant-local Iceberg rebuild is an architecture error\n\nThis deserves its own statement because it is not a style preference.\n\nA participant that builds its own `CatalogBuilder` / `RestCatalog` wiring, its\nown token refresh and its own Parquet writer has forked the catalog layer. The\nconsequences are not hypothetical: catalog credentials then live in two places,\nnamespace conventions drift apart, org scoping is enforced twice with two\ndifferent definitions of \"scoped\", and a schema fix has to be made twice by\nsomeone who has to know both copies exist.\n\n**This state exists today** in `sgh-acct/crates/sgh-acct-iceberg`:\n`handler.rs` imports `iceberg::{Catalog, CatalogBuilder}`,\n`RestCatalog`/`RestCatalogBuilder` with `REST_CATALOG_PROP_URI` /\n`REST_CATALOG_PROP_WAREHOUSE`, and drives `ParquetWriterBuilder` with its own\n`WriterProperties` — i.e. it reimplements what `sgh-s3iced` already serves.\n\nIt is recorded here as a **condition to be repaired**, not as a permitted\nvariant. The target is that `sgh-acct` reaches Iceberg exactly the way\n`sgh-flow` does: through an MCP adapter over `s3ice.*`.\n\n---\n\n## 8. sgh-acct — the invoice-accounting participant, not a second platform\n\n## 8.1 What sgh-acct is\n\n`sgh-acct` is a **participant**: a domain product that runs beside the\nplatform under the platform's participant contract.\n\n- process: `sgh-acctd`\n- manifest: `sgh-acct/participant.toml` (port `4610`, subject kind `invoice`,\n  route prefix `/acct`, own vault)\n- own database: `acctdb`\n- MCP namespace: `acct`\n- 6 crates in `sgh-acct/crates/` (config, db, error, iceberg, service, daemon)\n\nThe manifest is the single source for its systemd unit, env block and\ninfrastructure needs, and it deliberately contains **no** UUIDs — identities\nare derived or read back, never transcribed (the parser actively rejects\nUUID-shaped values). That rule is the same one chapter 14 states platform-wide.\n\n## 8.2 What sgh-acct owns\n\n`sgh-acct` owns the **operational invoice-data truth**:\n\n- invoice items, positions and their accounting assignment (Kontierung)\n- the master data the assignment resolves against: `sachkonto`, `kreditor`,\n  `cost_center`, `segment`, `department` — all in `acctdb`\n- the accounting-domain logic that turns a normalized invoice into booked lines\n- the `acct.*` MCP tools that expose those capabilities\n- its own agent wiring for AI-assisted accounting proposals\n\nThis is the strong, legitimate core of the participant: nobody else should\nhold the Kontierung tables or the accounting rules that read them.\n\n## 8.3 What sgh-acct must not become\n\nIt must not become:\n\n- **its own decision/audit truth.** Approval, decision history and audit\n  remain platform-owned. sgh-acct may *read* decisions; it does not become the\n  place where \"what was approved\" is authoritatively kept, because a second\n  authority for that question means neither answer can be trusted.\n- **its own Iceberg catalog.** See 7.5 — `sgh-acct-iceberg` is the concrete\n  drift to unwind, not the pattern to extend.\n- **its own vector-store operator.** Store lifecycle, embedding and retrieval\n  stay in vectory; sgh-acct is a consumer of retrieval, not a runner of it.\n- **the place where platform-wide tenant decisions are made.** Which org a\n  request belongs to, and whether that claim is trustworthy, is a platform\n  question. A participant enforces the scope it is handed; it does not invent\n  it.\n\n## 8.4 Tenant scope is verified, not asserted\n\n`sgh-acctd` derives the tenant scope from the signed `X-SGH-*` edge context, not\nfrom the request body. `verified_edge_scope_from_headers`\n(`sgh-acct/crates/sgh-acctd/src/app.rs`) checks an HMAC-SHA256 proof over the\norganisation, subject and timestamp, enforces a timestamp window, and is wired\ninto the `/mcp` handler before any tool dispatch. An empty or missing secret\nfails **closed** (`EdgeContextError::SecretNotConfigured`) — there is no bypass.\n\n`params._meta.organization_i\n\n[fs.read: Ausgabe gekürzt auf 16000 Bytes (Bytes 7000..23000 von 41003); weiterlesen mit offset=23000]"},"duration_ms":3,"trust":"untrusted"}}

      //! Canonical sandbox contract for work execution.
      //!
      //! This crate resolves configured workspace aliases into canonical filesystem
      //! roots and represents monotonic permission reduction. It deliberately does
      //! not execute processes, mount filesystems, or launch MCP servers: those
      //! backends must consume a frozen [`SandboxSpec`] at their syscall boundary.
      //!
      //! Autorität wird in zwei unabhängigen Achsen geführt, die beide nur schrumpfen
      //! können: [`PermissionSet`] beschreibt *welche Art* von Operation erlaubt ist,
      //! [`NetworkScope`] beschreibt *welche Hosts* eine bereits per
      //! [`Permission::NetworkAccess`] freigegebene Netzverbindung erreichen darf.
      //! Beide Achsen werden ausschließlich per Schnittmenge verengt; es gibt keine
      //! API, die einer Kind-Sandbox etwas zurückgibt, das der Elternteil nicht hat.
      //!
      //! Der ursprüngliche Ausbauplan sah für ausgehende Verbindungen einen neuen,
      //! zu [`NetworkScope`] parallelen Typ `EgressSet` vor. Eine Analyse des
      //! bestehenden Codes ergab: [`NetworkScope`] *ist bereits* der geforderte
      //! Halbverband — mit `intersection`, `is_subset_of`, punktgrenzen-geschütztem
      //! `allows` und Normalisierung in `from_hosts`, und ohne `add` oder
      //! Vereinigung. Ein zweiter Typ daneben wäre eine zweite Wahrheit über
      //! dieselbe Frage, mit demselben Risiko, auseinanderzulaufen. [`NetworkScope`]
      //! wurde deshalb um [`EgressTarget`] (Hostname, DNS-Suffix, CIDR-Bereich)

      //! bestehenden Namen.

      /// Operationsklassen, die eine Sandbox autorisieren kann.
      ///
      /// Es gibt bewusst keine Permission für beliebigen Dateisystemzugriff außerhalb
      /// des aufgelösten Workspace. Die einzige Ausnahme ist
      /// [`Permission::ReadCargoRegistry`]: sie benennt genau einen fest verdrahteten,
      /// nur lesbaren Pfad und keine vom Aufrufer wählbare Position.
      #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Serialize, Deserialize)]
      pub enum Permission {
          ReadWorkspace,
          WriteWorkspace,
          ExecuteProcess,
          /// Erlaubt ausgehende Netzverbindungen. Die zusätzliche Einschränkung auf
          /// einzelne Ziel-Hosts leistet [`NetworkScope`], nicht diese Permission.
          NetworkAccess,
          ReadSecrets,
          ManagePlugins,
          /// Lesezugriff auf die entpackten Abhängigkeitsquellen unter
          /// `$CARGO_HOME/registry/src`.
          ///
          /// # Beschreibung
          /// Gedacht für Dependency-Quellen-Recherche: ein Werkzeug darf den Code
          /// lesen, den der eigene Build ohnehin bereits kompiliert. Die Permission
          /// gewährt ausdrücklich **keinen** Schreibzugriff (auch nicht auf die
          /// Registry selbst), **keinen** Netzzugriff (Herunterladen oder Aktualisieren
          /// von Crates bleibt [`Permission::NetworkAccess`] vorbehalten) und hat
          /// **keinen** Bezug zum Workspace: der Pfad liegt außerhalb des Workspace und
          /// wird deshalb nie über [`WorkspaceBinding`] aufgelöst.
          ///
          /// # Hinweis für Backends
          /// Der Kern hält nur die Autorisierung. Ein Backend muss sie in eine reine
          /// Lesebindung des Registry-Pfads übersetzen; ohne diese Übersetzung bleibt
          /// die Permission wirkungslos (fail-closed).
          ReadCargoRegistry,
      }
      
      /// A permission set with no mutation API. It can only be built from a trusted
      /// policy decision and monotonically narrowed by intersection.
      #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
      pub struct PermissionSet {
          granted: BTreeSet<Permission>,
      }
      
      impl PermissionSet {
          #[must_use]
          pub fn empty() -> Self {
              Self {
                  granted: BTreeSet::new(),
              }
          }
      
          /// Constructs the result of a trusted policy evaluation. Channel and child
          /// code must subsequently call [`Self::intersection`], never re-grant.
          #[must_use]
          pub fn from_policy<I>(permissions: I) -> Self
          where
              I: IntoIterator<Item = Permission>,
          {
              Self {
                  granted: permissions.into_iter().collect(),
              }
          }
      
          #[must_use]
          pub fn contains(&self, permission: Permission) -> bool {
              self.granted.contains(&permission)
          }
      
          #[must_use]
          pub fn intersection(&self, other: &Self) -> Self {
              Self {
                  granted: self.granted.intersection(&other.granted).copied().collect(),
              }
          }
      
          #[must_use]
          pub fn is_subset_of(&self, parent: &Self) -> bool {
              self.granted.is_subset(&parent.granted)
          }
      
          pub fn iter(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = Permission> + '_ {
              self.granted.iter().copied()
          }
      }
      
      impl Default for PermissionSet {
          fn default() -> Self {
              Self::empty()
          }
      }
      
      /// Netzmodus eines Prozess-Sandkastens (W5 N-SBX, F-003/F-120).

      /// # Description
      /// Bestimmt, wie ein Bubblewrap-Backend Netz bereitstellt. Es gibt bewusst
      /// **keinen** Modus, der den Host-Netz-Namespace teilt (`--share-net`): jeder
      /// Modus erzeugt eine eigene, leere netns (`--unshare-net`).
      ///
      /// - [`NetworkMode::None`] (Default): keine Netzverbindung, nur `lo`.
      /// - [`NetworkMode::ProxyOnly`]: in derselben netns läuft `harw-netns-relay`
      ///   auf `127.0.0.1:<listen_port>` und leitet an den Unix-Socket des
      ///   Egress-Proxys im Harness weiter; der Kindprozess erhält
      ///   `ALL_PROXY=socks5h://127.0.0.1:<listen_port>`. Erfordert zusätzlich
      ///   [`Permission::NetworkAccess`].
      ///
      /// # Concurrency
      /// Reiner Wert (`Send + Sync`), keine Seiteneffekte.
      ///
      /// # Examples
      /// ```rust
      /// use harw_sandbox::NetworkMode;
      ///
      /// assert_eq!(NetworkMode::default(), NetworkMode::None);
      /// ```
      #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
      pub enum NetworkMode {
          /// Eigene netns ohne Außenverbindung.
          #[default]
          None,
          /// Eigene netns; Ausgang nur über Relay → Egress-Proxy.
          ProxyOnly(RelaySpec),
      }

## Assistant

Deine Priorität ist richtig: `PermissionSet::from_policy` ist aktuell öffentlich und kann damit von jeder abhängigen Crate neue Rechte erzeugen. Das unterläuft das sonst monotone Modell (`intersection`/`restrict`).

Aber: `pub(crate)` ist hier nicht nur ein kleiner Sichtbarkeitswechsel. Der Konstruktor wird bereits in mindestens 48 Rust-Dateien verwendet, darunter zahlreiche Produktions-Crates (`harw-runtime`, `harw-core`, `harw-ops`, Tool-Crates, Registry). `pub(crate)` gilt nur innerhalb von `harw-sandbox` und würde diese Aufrufer sofort brechen.

Die passende Priorisierung wäre daher:

1. Alle legitimen Erzeugungspunkte als „Policy-/Assembly-Grenze“ festlegen.
2. Konstruktion dorthin verlagern bzw. über eine eng begrenzte Factory kapseln.
3. Erst dann `from_policy` auf `pub(crate)` ziehen und alle übrigen Stellen ausschließlich über Schnittmengen reduzieren.

Das schließt tatsächlich die offene Rechteflanke; ein bloßes Sichtbarkeits-Commit ohne Migration würde nur den Workspace unbaubar machen.

      ---
      name: brainstorming
      description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation."
      ---
      
      # Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs
      
      Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.
      
      Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
      through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
      design, and get your human partner's approval.
      
      <HARD-GATE>
      Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
      project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
      human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
      to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
      the approval gate never does.
      </HARD-GATE>
      
      ## Three Paths
      
      Before your first question, classify the request and say the
      classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
      design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
      override it:
      
      - **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
        "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
        keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
        a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
        doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
        built stays labeled throwaway.
      - **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
        this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
        Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
        you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
        flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
        questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
        sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
        starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
        bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
        one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
      - **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
        restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
        depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
        design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
      
      When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
      one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
      stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
      
      ## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
      
      Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
      implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
      change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
      it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
      cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
      artifact, never the approval.
      
      ## Red Flags
      
      | Thought | Reality |
      |---------|---------|
      | "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
      | "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
      | "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
      | "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
      | "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
      | "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
      | "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
      
      ## Checklist
      
      Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
      your path and complete them in order.
      
      **Spike:**
      1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
      2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
      3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
      4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
      5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway
      
      **Bounded:**
      1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
      2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
      3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
      4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
      5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document
      
      **Architectural:**
      1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
      2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
      3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
      4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
      5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
      6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
      7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
      8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
      9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan
      
      ## Process Flow
      
      ```dot
      digraph brainstorming {
          "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
          "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
          "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
          "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
          "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
          "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
          "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];
          "Explore project context" [shape=box];
          "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
          "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
          "Present design sections" [shape=box];
          "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
          "Write design doc" [shape=box];
          "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
          "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
          "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];
          "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" [shape=box];
      
          "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [label="spike"];
          "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
          "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];
          "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" -> "Human approves?";
          "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" -> "Present short design in chat";
          "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
          "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
          "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
          "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
          "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
          "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
          "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
          "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
          "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
          "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
          "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
          "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
          "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
          "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
      }
      ```
      
      **Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
      invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
      mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
      approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
      development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
      reported recommendation.
      
      ## The Process
      
      The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
      spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
      **Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
      bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
      is the whole process.
      
      **Understanding the idea:**
      
      - Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
      - Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
      - If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
      - For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
      - Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
      - Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
      - Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
      
      **Exploring approaches:**
      
      - Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
      - Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
      - Lead with your recommended option and explain why
      - YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
      
      **Presenting the design:**
      
      - Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
      - Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
      - Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
      - Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
      - Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
      
      **Design for isolation and clarity:**
      
      - Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
      - For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
      - Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
      - Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
      
      **Working in existing codebases:**
      
      - Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
      - Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
      - Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
      
      ## After the Design (architectural path)
      
      **Documentation:**
      
      - Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
        - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
      - Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
      - Commit the design document to git
      
      **Spec Self-Review:**
      After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
      
      1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
      2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
      3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
      4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
      
      Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
      
      **User Review Gate:**
      After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
      
      > "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
      
      Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
      
      **Implementation:**
      
      - Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
      - Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.
      
      ## Visual Companion
      
      A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
      
      **Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
      > "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."
      
      **This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.
      
      **Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
      
      - **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
      - **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
      
      A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
      
      If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
      `skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
      ---
      name: writing-plans
      description: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code
      ---
      
      # Writing Plans
      
      ## Overview
      
      Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.
      
      Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.
      
      **Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."
      
      **Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.
      
      **Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
      - (User preferences for plan location override this default)
      
      ## Scope Check
      
      If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.
      
      ## File Structure
      
      Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.
      
      - Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
      - You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
      - Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
      - In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.
      
      This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.
      
      ## Task Right-Sizing
      
      A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
      fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
      configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
      deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
      reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
      independently testable deliverable.
      
      ## Bite-Sized Task Granularity
      
      **Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
      - "Write the failing test" - step
      - "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
      - "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
      - "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
      - "Commit" - step
      
      ## Plan Document Header
      
      **Every plan MUST start with this header:**
      
      ```markdown
      # [Feature Name] Implementation Plan
      
      > **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.
      
      **Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]
      
      **Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]
      
      **Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]
      
      **Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
      argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]
      
      ## Global Constraints
      
      [The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
      naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
      values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
      include this section.]
      
      ---
      ```
      
      ## Task Structure
      
      ````markdown
      ### Task N: [Component Name]
      
      **Files:**
      - Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
      - Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
      - Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`
      
      **Interfaces:**
      - Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
      - Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
        and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
        block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]
      
      - [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**
      
      ```python
      def test_specific_behavior():
          result = function(input)
          assert result == expected
      ```
      
      - [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**
      
      Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
      Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"
      
      - [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**
      
      ```python
      def function(input):
          return expected
      ```
      
      - [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**
      
      Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
      Expected: PASS
      
      - [ ] **Step 5: Commit**
      
      ```bash
      git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
      git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
      ```
      ````
      
      ## No Placeholders
      
      Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
      - "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
      - "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
      - "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
      - "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
      - Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
      - References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task
      
      ## Self-Review
      
      After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.
      
      **1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.
      
      **2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.
      
      **3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.
      
      If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.
      
      ## Execution Handoff
      
      After saving the plan, offer execution choice:
      
      **"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**
      
      **1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration
      
      **2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints
      
      **Which approach?"**
      
      **If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
      - **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
      - Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review
      
      **If Inline Execution chosen:**
      - **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
      - Batch execution with checkpoints for review

Eine Facade hilft folglich dessen Crates, aber aktiviert oder härtet DoD selbst noch nicht.

## Assistant

Für diesen Rechner gibt es bereits zwei getrennte Binärpfade: `harw-sentinel` ist bewusst unprivilegiert; `harw-warden` besitzt die cgroup-/Durchsetzungsseite und Socket-Aktivierung. Die vorhandene Konfiguration setzt Kill ohnehin auf menschliche Freigabe, aber Auto-Freeze ist derzeit möglich — das müssen wir für den ersten Lauf bewusst festlegen.
